books.section: Topic 4.12 African Americans in the Early Republic, B. The Cultures of African-American Communities

primary_sources: Richard Allen, founder of the African Methodist Episcopal Church, 1816

stimulus.text:
The church: In 1816, Richard Allen and other Black Methodist ministers in Philadelphia formed the African Methodist Episcopal Church, the first independent Black denomination in the United States. Allen, who had bought his own freedom from slavery, became its first bishop. Black Methodists had left white-led churches after Black worshippers were pulled from their knees at prayer.

The speaker: "Tell us no more of southern slavery; for with few exceptions, although I may be very erroneous in my opinion, yet I consider our condition but little better than that." — Maria W. Stewart, speaking at Franklin Hall, Boston, September 21, 1832.

The school: In 1833, Prudence Crandall, a white Quaker teacher, opened a school for Black girls in Canterbury, Connecticut. Townspeople attacked the school and forced it to close in 1834.

The stories and songs: Enslaved people told Br’er Rabbit stories, in which the weak rabbit outwits the strong, and made music on fiddles and banjos built from gourds and horsehair, mixing African and Southern traditions.
stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.12 B, with the Stewart quotation verbatim from her September 21, 1832 address at Franklin Hall, Boston, and the Crandall facts checked against the Oxford African American Studies Center chronology.

source: original; stimulus paraphrased from Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.12 B
stem: The founding of the African Methodist Episcopal Church in 1816 best shows that free Black Americans

options.text: rejected Christianity and returned to African religions
options.misconception: They kept the Methodist faith and built a Methodist church.

options.text: waited for white churches to grant them equal seats
options.misconception: They left and built their own church.

options.text: moved to Africa to build churches in Liberia
options.misconception: The church was founded in Philadelphia.

options.text: built their own institutions instead of accepting second-class treatment

rationales.A: Allen and his people stayed Methodist. They built a Methodist denomination of their own, they did not leave the faith.
rationales.B: They did not wait. After being pulled from prayer in a white-led church, they formed a church of their own.
rationales.C: The AME Church began in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, not in Liberia.
rationales.D: Black Methodists formed their own denomination, with Allen as its first bishop, instead of accepting a second-class place.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what Allen did. He gathered Black Methodist churches into a denomination of their own.
2. Ask why. Black worshippers had been pulled from their knees at prayer in a white-led church.
3. Name the move. Independence, not waiting.
Background: Allen bought his own freedom and became the church’s first bishop.
Remember: when people build their own institution, ask what the old one denied them.
